title: Bus, train, taxi
topic: the prepositions בְּ־ לְ־ מִ־ with the article (בַּ־ לַ־ מֵהַ־); transportation
why: You learn to combine בְּ, לְ and מִ with the article (בַּ, לַ, מֵהַ), where Hebrew fuses "in the," "to the," and "from the" into a single word, plus the vocabulary of transportation. It's the foundation for taking the bus or the train in the next lessons.

In the, to the: בַּ־ and לַ־

English keeps \"in\" and \"the\" as two separate words. Hebrew merges them: when בְּ (in, at) or לְ (to, toward) meets the article הַ, the ה disappears and the preposition takes its vowel.

Preposition + articleResultMeaning
בְּ + הַבַּיִתבַּבַּיִת ba-bayitat home (in the house)
בְּ + הַשּׁוּקבַּשּׁוּק ba-shukat the market (inside)
לְ + הַיָּםלַיָּם la-yamto the sea (direction)
לְ + הַתַּחֲנָהלַתַּחֲנָה la-takhanato the stop (direction)

The dot inside the letter (בַּשּׁוּק) stays, just as after הַ. If the article is הָ (before א, ע, ר), the preposition also takes ָ: הָעִיר → בָּעִיר (in town), לָעִיר.

Without the article, the preposition keeps its shva: בְּבַנְק (in a bank), לְחֵיפָה (to Haifa). Before another shva, it becomes בִּ / לִ: לִירוּשָׁלַיִם (lirushalayim, to Jerusalem).

", "

From the: מֵהַ־

מִ (from, since) is the exception: it doesn't swallow the article. It becomes מֵ and the הַ stays.

אֲנִי בָּא מֵהַתַּחֲנָה.I'm coming from the stop. [ani ba me-ha-takhana.]
מֵהַשּׁוּק לַיָּם זֶה עֶשֶׂר דַּקּוֹת.From the market to the sea, it's ten minutes. [me-ha-shuk la-yam ze eser dakot.]

Without the article, you already know it: מִפָּרִיז, מִתֵּל אָבִיב. To sum up: בַּ = in the, לַ = to the, toward the, מֵהַ = from the.

For transportation, Hebrew says \"in the bus\": בָּאוֹטוֹבּוּס (by bus), בָּרַכֶּבֶת (by train), בְּמוֹנִית (by taxi).

", "

Bus, train, taxi

HebrewPronunciationMeaning
אוֹטוֹבּוּסotobusbus
רַכֶּבֶתrakevettrain (f.)
מוֹנִיתmonittaxi (f.)
קַוkavline
רַב־קַוrav-kavthe transit card

To find your bus, there's just one sentence to learn, as a single block:

אֵיזֶה קַו נוֹסֵעַ לַמֶּרְכָּז?Which line goes to the center? [eize kav nose'a la-merkaz?]

אֵיזֶה (which, m.) goes with a masculine noun, אֵיזוֹ (which, f.) with a feminine one: אֵיזוֹ רַכֶּבֶת? In speech, many people say אֵיזֶה for everything. The line number is said with the counting numbers: קַו חָמֵשׁ (line 5).

The רַב־קַו is the rechargeable card valid throughout the country; drivers generally no longer sell tickets. In most cities, buses and trains don't run during Shabbat, from Friday afternoon to Saturday evening.
